idiom_name: opaque struct handle with a const identity member and a hand-written equality function
implementation_notes: C has no methods, no operator overloading and no automatic struct equality, so the classic structure is written by hand: declare an opaque typedef (struct customer is defined only in the implementation file), give the struct a const identity member, and expose create/reconstitute functions as the only places where identity is set. Since C does not compare structs with == and memcmp is unreliable because padding bytes are indeterminate, equality is an explicit function comparing identities only, and a table keyed by id keeps one instance per identity. The opaque handle is worth keeping even for simple entities: it stops callers from copying state and identity independently, which is exactly what makes struct assignment unsafe here.
pitfalls: Assigning the struct by value copies the identity together with the state, so two variables can claim the same id; keep entities behind opaque handles or pointers and copy state only through the API.
memcmp or == on the struct is not equality: C structs have no automatic comparison, and padding bytes make byte-wise comparison unreliable.
A provisional identifier that is replaced after insert forks the identity; if the storage layer assigns the key, return the entity with the final id and never hand out the temporary one.
